passages.happening:
“Now this is what you are to do to consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests: Take a young bull and two rams without blemish” (verse 1), with unleavened bread, cakes and wafers in a basket (verses 2-3).

“Then present Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water” (verse 4). Aaron is dressed in the garments of chapter 28 (verses 5-6). “Then take the anointing oil and anoint him by pouring it on his head” (verse 7). His sons are dressed too (verses 8-9). “The priesthood shall be theirs by a permanent statute. In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 28 described the priests' clothes. This chapter tells how the men who wear them are to be set apart. The ceremony is carried out later, in Leviticus 8, after the tabernacle is built.

Every step had a meaning the first hearers knew. Washing meant cleansing before coming into a holy place. Clothing meant taking on an office. Anointing with oil set a person apart for a special role. Kings were anointed too. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is the source of the title Messiah, and the Greek word for it gives us Christ.

Aaron does nothing to make himself a priest. He is brought, washed, dressed and anointed. The office is given, not taken.
passages.later:
Hebrews says of the priesthood, “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4).

Leviticus tells how it was done: “Moses took some of the anointing oil and some of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled them on Aaron and his garments” (Leviticus 8:30).
passages.asks: Aaron was washed and clothed before he could serve. Ask whether you try to make yourself fit for God, or let him make you fit. And ask what it means that the title Christ means the Anointed One.

passages.t: A sin offering and a burnt offering
passages.happening:
Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the bull's head, and it is killed at the entrance to the tent (verses 10-11). Some of its blood goes on the horns of the altar, and the rest is poured out at its base (verse 12). The fat is burned on the altar, “But burn the flesh of the bull and its hide and dung outside the camp; it is a sin offering” (verses 13-14).

Then a ram. They lay their hands on its head, it is killed, and its blood is sprinkled on the altar (verses 15-16). “Then burn the entire ram on the altar; it is a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The ceremony uses three sacrifices, in a clear order. First a sin offering, to deal with impurity. Then a burnt offering, burned whole, a sign of complete giving to God. Then, in the next verses, the ram of ordination, shared as a meal.

The men about to become priests need cleansing first themselves. They lay their hands on the animal's head. That gesture joined the one making the offering with the animal being offered.

The sin offering's body is burned outside the camp. The burnt offering goes up entirely in smoke, ‘a pleasing aroma’ to God.

Sacrifice was the common language of worship in the ancient world. Temples in Egypt, Mesopotamia and Canaan all offered animals, grain and drink to their gods. The Old Testament takes up that language and fills it with Israel's knowledge of God. The sacrifices were not food for a hungry god, and they were not bribes. They were God's own provision for cleansing, giving and fellowship. They taught that sin is serious, that it costs life, and that God himself provides the way back.
passages.later:
God mocks the idea that he needs food: “Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Psalm 50:13). And the prophets insisted that sacrifice without a changed heart was worthless: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

Hebrews says of the bodies burned outside the camp, “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).
passages.hard:
Why did God require animal sacrifice, and how should Christians read these rites now?

Animal sacrifice can seem strange or troubling today. In the ancient world it was how people everywhere worshiped, and the Bible uses that language while changing what it means: the sacrifices were not food for God or a way to buy him off, but his gift, teaching that sin is costly and that he provides the way back.

Christians read these chapters in the light of Christ. Most traditions hold that the sacrifices have been fulfilled and ended by his death, as Hebrews argues, so that they are no longer offered but still teach about sin, holiness and grace. Jewish tradition, after the temple was destroyed in AD 70, came to stress prayer, study of the Torah and deeds of kindness in place of sacrifice. Readers in both traditions find in these chapters what it means for a holy God to live among people.
passages.asks: The priests needed cleansing before they could serve others. Ask whether you try to help others while ignoring your own need of God's mercy. And ask what it would mean to give yourself to God wholly, like the burnt offering, holding nothing back.

passages.t: Blood on ear, thumb and toe
passages.happening:
The second ram is the ram of ordination. They lay their hands on it, and it is killed (verses 19-20). “take some of its blood, and put it on the right earlobes of Aaron and his sons, on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet” (verse 20). Blood from the altar and anointing oil are sprinkled on them and their garments, “Then he and his garments will be consecrated” (verse 21).

Parts of the ram, with bread from the basket, are put in their hands and waved before the LORD, then burned (verses 22-25). The breast and the thigh become the priests' share, “a regular portion from the Israelites” (verses 26-28).
passages.hearers:
This is the most striking moment of the ceremony. Blood is put on the right ear, the right thumb and the right big toe.

The text does not explain it. Interpreters commonly read it as setting apart the whole person: the ear that hears God's word, the hand that serves, the foot that walks. The same marking is used when someone healed of a skin disease is cleansed and brought back into the community.

Then Moses puts parts of the offering into their hands. The Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest is, word for word, to fill the hand. Here Moses does it literally.

The fat was burned for God. The breast and thigh went to the priests. That is how Israel supported its priests: they lived from the offerings they served. The ‘fat tail’ belonged to the broad-tailed sheep of the region, whose tail stored fat and was counted a choice part.
passages.later:
Leviticus uses the same marking for a person cleansed from a skin disease: the priest puts blood “on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot” (Leviticus 14:14).

Paul calls every believer to a whole-person offering: “offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship” (Romans 12:1).
passages.asks: Ear, hand and foot were all set apart for God. Ask whether there is any part of your life you keep back from him: what you listen to, what you do, where you go. And ask how the people who serve you in the faith are cared for.

passages.happening:
Aaron's holy garments will pass to his sons after him (verses 29-30). The ram of ordination is boiled in a holy place, and Aaron and his sons eat it with the bread at the entrance to the tent (verses 31-32). “They must eat those things by which atonement was made for their ordination and consecration. But no outsider may eat them, because these things are sacred” (verse 33).

The ceremony takes seven days, with a bull for a sin offering each day (verses 35-36). “For seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it. Then the altar will become most holy; whatever touches the altar will be holy” (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
The ordination ends with a meal. The new priests eat from the offering that made atonement for them. Being set apart for God ends at his table.

The garments pass from father to son. The priesthood is a family's service, handed down.

Seven days is a full week. Even the altar must be cleansed and set apart, day after day, before it can be used.

‘Whatever touches the altar will be holy.’ What comes into contact with the altar now belongs to God.
passages.later:
John's Gospel tells how Jesus prayed for his followers before his death, “Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth” (John 17:17). To sanctify is to set apart for God, the work this chapter does for the priests.

Luke opens his Gospel with a priest of Aaron's line on duty: “he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense” (Luke 1:9).
passages.asks: The priests' setting apart took seven days, not a moment. Ask whether you expect God to change you all at once, or are willing for it to take time. And ask what it means to you that holy service began with a meal at God's table.

passages.t: Morning and evening, ‘and be their God’
passages.happening:
“This is what you are to offer regularly on the altar, each day: two lambs that are a year old. Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight” (verses 38-39), with flour, oil and wine (verses 40-41).

This offering is to be made “at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, where I will meet you to speak with you” (verse 42). “I will also meet with the Israelites there, and that place will be consecrated by My glory” (verse 43).

“Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God. And they will know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God” (verses 45-46).
passages.hearers:
Every morning and every evening, one lamb. This daily offering was called the tamid, the regular offering. It was offered at the temple in Jerusalem for centuries, and when it was stopped, the loss was felt as a disaster.

Then the chapter rises to the high point of all the tabernacle instructions. God is the subject of every verb: I will meet, I will consecrate, I will dwell. And the reason for the whole exodus is said plainly: God brought them out of Egypt ‘so that I might dwell among them’.

The exodus was not only an escape from slavery. It was so that God could live with his people.

The words ‘they will know that I am the LORD’ ran through the plague stories, where Egypt learned it through judgment. Now Israel will learn it through God's presence among them.

That promise is about to be tested. In chapter 32 the people make a golden calf. In chapter 40 the glory fills the tent all the same.
passages.later:
Daniel saw a power that “removed His daily sacrifice and overthrew the place of His sanctuary” (Daniel 8:11).

Hebrews contrasts the daily offerings with Christ's one offering (Hebrews 10:11-12). John says the Word “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). And Revelation ends with the promise of this verse fulfilled: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).
passages.asks: Morning and evening, every day, the people's worship rose to God. Ask what rhythm of prayer marks your days. And ask what it means to you that God's purpose in rescuing you was not only to free you, but to live with you.
